notes.meaning: Solomon began building the temple 480 years after Israel came out of Egypt, during the spring of his fourth year as king. This date showed that the long era of wandering with a portable tent was finally coming to a close in the promised land. Solomon spent his first three years preparing workers and materials so construction could begin smoothly.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some scholars note that 480 may represent twelve symbolic generations of forty years, which would place the Exodus in the 1200s BC around the time of Ramesses II rather than the 1400s BC.

notes.meaning: The main temple building was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high (about ninety feet long, thirty feet wide, and forty-five feet high). It doubled the length and width of the desert tabernacle, showing continuity with Israel's past worship. The building was not huge compared to pagan palaces, because its true value came from the presence of God.

The entry porch at the front of the temple was twenty cubits wide, matching the width of the main building. It extended forward ten cubits toward the east. This entry hall served as a welcoming vestibule before the sacred rooms within.

Narrow latticed windows were set high up along the temple walls. These openings allowed smoke from the golden lamps and burning incense to escape while admitting fresh air and sunlight. They also pointed forward to how Old Testament worship gave a shadowy foretaste of full gospel light.

A three-story structure of side rooms was built against the outer walls of the temple on three sides. Each floor became one cubit wider than the floor below it because the temple wall stepped in, forming exterior ledges. These ledges supported the ceiling beams so that no timber had to be hammered into the sacred walls of the temple itself.

Every stone was cut and shaped at the quarry so that it arrived at the building site ready to be put in place. As a result, no hammer, axe, or iron tool was heard at the temple hill during construction. This quiet atmosphere honored the God of peace and pictured how God gently shapes believers in this life to fit His heavenly home.

The entrance to the lowest floor of side rooms opened on the south side of the building. Inside, a winding staircase led priests up to the second and third stories. These rooms provided orderly, quiet storage for priestly vestments and temple vessels.

Solomon finished the outer frame of the temple and roofed it over with sturdy cedar beams and planks. Alongside the main structure, he completed the side chambers, which stood five cubits high per level and rested securely against the walls. Cedar from Lebanon was chosen for its strength, pleasant scent, and lasting beauty.

While construction was underway, God spoke a direct word of promise and warning to Solomon. The Lord promised to dwell among the people of Israel and uphold the throne of David, but only if Solomon lived in faithful obedience to His commandments. A magnificent house of stone and gold could never replace real devotion or protect an unfaithful nation from judgment.

Encouraged by God's word, Solomon pressed forward with the building project until it was finished. He did not grow weary of the enormous cost or leave the task half done. He worked steadily with wisdom until the structure stood complete.

The interior stone walls were paneled with cedar wood from the floor to the ceiling beams. The sanctuary floor was covered with boards of durable cypress wood. Inside the temple, the cold stone was hidden completely behind warm and fragrant timber.

Solomon set apart the back twenty cubits of the building using cedar boards to form the Most Holy Place, the inner sanctuary. In front of it was the main hall, known as the Holy Place, which was forty cubits long. This two-room layout matched the design of the wilderness tabernacle.

Carvings of wild gourds and blossoming flowers covered the cedar paneling throughout the sanctuary. Every surface was carved so that no bare stone could be seen anywhere inside. These rich plant figures pictured life, beauty, and fruitfulness flourishing in God's presence.

The inner room was specifically prepared to hold the ark of the covenant of the Lord. Inside this sacred chest were the two stone tablets containing the Ten Commandments. The ark had traveled with Israel since the days of Moses, and it remained the supreme earthly symbol of God's holy presence.

The Most Holy Place formed a perfect cube, measuring twenty cubits in length, width, and height. Solomon covered every part of its interior walls with fine gold, and he also overlaid the cedar incense altar. The cube shape symbolized completeness and the perfection of God's heavenly kingdom.

Solomon overlaid the entire inside of the temple with pure gold and hung golden chains across the entrance of the inner sanctuary. He also covered the incense altar that stood before this sacred room with gold. The bright gold and heavy chains emphasized the majesty of God and the reverence needed when approaching Him.

Inside the Most Holy Place, Solomon placed two large winged cherub figures carved from olive wood. Each cherub stood ten cubits high (about fifteen feet) and had two wings measuring five cubits each, creating a full wingspan of ten cubits. Both sculptures were crafted with identical size, shape, and proportions.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the cherubim were winged creatures with animal bodies and human faces, similar to guardian figures found in neighboring ancient Near Eastern temples.

notes.meaning: The two cherubim were set side by side in the inner sanctuary and covered completely with gold. With their wings outstretched, one wing of each figure touched an outer wall while their inner wingtips met in the center of the room. Beneath their wide wings, the ark of the covenant rested in quiet safety.

Carved engravings of cherubim, palm trees, and open blossoms decorated the walls of both the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place. The cherubim represented the heavenly angels who worship and serve God, while the palm trees and flowers pointed to flourishing life. Together these carvings created an image of God's house as a restored garden of paradise.

The entire wooden floor was overlaid with plates of gold throughout both the outer and inner rooms. Walking on gold showed that earthly treasures are meant to serve the honor of God. It also foreshadowed the heavenly city of God, whose streets are described as pure gold.

Solomon built two-leaved doors of olive wood to form the entrance into the Most Holy Place. He carved them with cherubim, palm trees, and flowers, and covered the carvings with carefully hammered gold. These magnificent doors guarded the room where only the high priest was allowed to enter once a year.

For the doorway into the main hall, Solomon made doorposts of olive wood and two folding doors out of cypress wood. Each cypress door had two turning panels and was decorated with carved cherubim, palms, and flowers coated in gold. Cypress was chosen because it was lighter than olive wood, allowing the doors to open easily for the priests' daily duties.

The inner courtyard where the priests offered sacrifices was built with three rows of cut stone topped by a row of cedar beams. This wall was kept low enough that the people standing in the outer court could see what was happening and hear the priests. It maintained orderly reverence while keeping the worshippers close to the service of God.

The foundation was laid in the spring of Solomon's fourth year, and the whole temple was finished down to the last detail in the autumn of his eleventh year. The entire project took seven and a half years, rounded here to seven years. Because Solomon had thousands of skilled workers and shaped the materials in advance, he was able to finish this magnificent sanctuary quickly.
